prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and its experimental discovery in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: Topological insulators changed how we classify electronic matter: Kane and Mele introduced the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall state with protected edge channels, and Molenkamp's HgTe experiment showed that this was a clue found in nature and not only an elegant idea. That theory-then-experiment chain is the kind of discovery I want at the centre of a prize. It has been reproduced for roughly two decades in transport and spectroscopy, and it fed into 3D topological insulators, materials science and ideas for quantum devices. After reading the other ballots, B053 is the only shortlisted candidate that four colleagues put in their top four and that nobody calls premature. Several members call it mature or even overdue.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the real weakness. Three names cannot cover Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan, and also Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who proposed HgTe and sit outside the credited names. Dropping Hasan removes the 3D branch of the field, and dropping Zhang leaves a visible gap in the HgTe chain. The 2016 prize to Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz also recognised topology in condensed matter, so some will see this as a continuation rather than a new area. Only five members ranked B053, so it lacks broad support. If the committee cannot settle the credit, B015 or B054 would be a cleaner choice.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks magic-angle graphene first because the Bistritzer-MacDonald model is a simple mechanism with universal consequences, and he considers the field mature enough and recognition timely.
responses.response: I share his taste for simple models, and I put B015 fifth only because of timing. Correlated states were first seen in 2018, and he himself says the superconducting mechanism is unresolved, so the prize would have to be phrased around the platform. Mehlig also says B053 is overdue, and I take that seriously. I agree with him that the main allocation problem is Hasan against Molenkamp, and I still prefer the 2D chain because the HgTe experiment is the cleaner complement to Kane and Mele.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B053 second and proposes Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, which leaves out Mele and values the ARPES identification of 3D topological insulators.
responses.response: Hasan's photoemission work is a real discovery, and I accept that the 3D branch is where much of the later materials science came from. But Kane and Mele wrote the paper that started the subject, and dropping Mele from the pair seems the least defensible cut to me. Eriksson himself concedes that this allocation is contestable. I would rather credit the foundational theory pair plus the first experimental observation than split the theory credit. If the committee wants 3D in the citation, Hasan would have to replace Molenkamp, and that has a cost: the prize then has no direct experimental confirmation of the 2D effect.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B015 first and B053 second, and for B053 she would credit the decisive experiments plus the foundational theory, while noting that Mele is left out of her version.
responses.response: We agree on the principle of crediting the foundational theory and the decisive experiment. Her own ballot shows the difficulty, since her trio omits Mele, who co-authored the Kane-Mele proposal. I think a three-name list that splits Kane and Mele misstates the history. I would also like to hear from her whether she thinks that the first magic-angle experiments are enough on their own, before the mechanism of the superconductivity is understood.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as a new observational window with durable detector and systematics work, but accepts that the source-physics story is still maturing and that credit is hard to allocate.
responses.response: I ranked B054 second and respect the case. The 2013 diffuse flux is secure and it opens a new window. My reservation is the same as his: the credited three do not map cleanly onto a collaboration with the AMANDA and Baikal lineage, and he suggests that a two-person Halzen-Karle prize may be fairer than adding Spiering. I think B053 has a clearer credit chain, but I would not oppose IceCube if the committee prefers an astroparticle prize.

uncertainties: Whether Hasan should replace Molenkamp, or whether Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang should be weighed against Mele, since the three-person limit forces a choice.
Whether the committee regards topological insulators as sufficiently distinct from the topological phase transitions honoured in 2016.
Whether magic-angle graphene will be seen as ripe, since the superconducting mechanism is unresolved and the field is eight years old.
I rely on my own recollection of the credit history, since the committee files give no independent verification of individual roles.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. My supervisor David Gross and my frequent co-author Thomas Van Riet are not connected to these candidates, and I have no known connection to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan or the other credited people.
